finding.summary: Cross-tenant leak: cacheKey() hashes only topK and the lowercased query, but searchChunks scopes the pgvector query by tenantId. searchChunks returns the cached hit before the tenant-filtered SQL runs, so tenant B asking the same question within 900s gets tenant A's chunks.
finding.evidence: cacheKey(query, topK) in cache.ts has no tenantId input; search.ts calls cacheKey(query, topK), then 'if (hit) return hit' ahead of the 'WHERE tenant_id = $1' query, and putCached stores rows under that shared key with a 900s TTL.

finding.summary: The retrieval cache is shared by all tenants, so entries should be namespaced per tenant or results may be visible to the wrong customer.
finding.evidence: The cache is a single DynamoDB table keyed by pk; the key does not look tenant-aware.

finding.summary: Lowercasing and trimming the query in the cache key makes 'Apple' and 'apple' collide, so a user can get chunks computed for a differently-cased query, which is a correctness bug in the cache.
finding.evidence: cacheKey applies query.trim().toLowerCase() before hashing, so differently-cased queries share one entry.

finding.summary: AGENT_TIMEOUT_S was raised to 900s but receive_message still passes VisibilityTimeout=60 and nothing extends visibility. After 60s the message becomes visible again and a second worker starts the same run while the first continues; the config note says DLQ redrive at 3 receives, so a healthy long run can be moved to the DLQ while still in flight.
finding.evidence: In consumer.py the timeout is 900 (line 12) while the receive_message call keeps VisibilityTimeout=60 and the loop has no ChangeMessageVisibility or heartbeat; delete_message only runs after run_agent returns, and config.py documents maxReceiveCount-style DLQ redrive.

finding.summary: The agent timeout is now 900 seconds but the SQS visibility timeout is still 60 seconds, so messages can be redelivered while a run is still going.
finding.evidence: Compares the two constants but does not trace the duplicate execution or DLQ consequence.

finding.summary: On TimeoutError the loop does 'continue' without deleting the message, so a timed-out run is retried forever and burns tokens indefinitely.
finding.evidence: The except TimeoutError branch logs and continues without delete_message, so the message reappears after the visibility timeout.

finding.summary: The MAX_DEPTH guard never trips for follow-ups: handle() reads msg.get('depth', 0), but enqueue_followup builds a new payload with only tenant_id, run_id and goal (no depth) and handle never increments it. Every follow-up arrives at depth 0, so a model that keeps returning needs_more_work creates an unbounded chain of queue messages.
finding.evidence: followup.py payload dict has three keys and omits depth; handler.py line 11 defaults depth to 0 and the 'depth >= MAX_DEPTH' check at line 12 therefore always sees 0; no code adds depth + 1 before enqueue_followup.

finding.summary: The recursion limit on follow-up steps is ineffective, so a run can keep re-enqueueing itself without bound.
finding.evidence: Bare assertion that the depth limit does not work, no trace of why.

finding.summary: The follow-up reuses the same run_id, so if the queue is FIFO with content-based deduplication the follow-up will be dropped as a duplicate and multi-step runs silently stall.
finding.evidence: payload copies msg['run_id'] into the follow-up message.

finding.summary: Conversation state moved from load_state/save_state into a per-process _SESSIONS dict while desiredCount goes from 1 to 4 behind the load balancer. Consecutive turns of one session hit different tasks with different (empty) history, and any restart or deploy loses all in-flight conversations including pending_tool_use. State is neither shared nor durable.
finding.evidence: conversation.py defines module-level _SESSIONS and get_state; chat.py drops load_state and save_state; api_service.ts changes desiredCount 1 -> 4 with no session affinity or shared store in the diff.

finding.summary: Keeping conversation history in an in-process dict means it is lost whenever the API process restarts, so it is not durable.
finding.evidence: Notes the _SESSIONS dict is volatile but does not connect it to the scale-out to four tasks or the removed save_state.

finding.summary: get_state uses _SESSIONS.setdefault from concurrent request handlers, so two simultaneous first requests for a session race and one request's ConversationState is overwritten, losing messages.
finding.evidence: setdefault on a shared module-level dict is called from the async chat route.

finding.summary: Exactly-once is not achieved: enqueueRun retries SendMessage with the same body after an ambiguous failure, so two messages with the same runId but different SQS messageIds can be enqueued. runConsumer dedupes on record.messageId rather than the runId in the body, so both pass the conditional put and the agent run executes twice.
finding.evidence: enqueueRun.ts builds body once with runId and re-sends it up to 3 times; runConsumer.ts uses pk msg#${record.messageId} for the ConditionExpression and never reads runId from JSON.parse(record.body).

finding.summary: The dedupe marker is written to DynamoDB before runAgent runs and is never removed on failure. If the Lambda crashes or runAgent throws after the marker is written, SQS redelivers the message, the conditional put fails and the record is skipped, so the run is lost.
finding.evidence: The PutItem precedes 'await runAgent'; ConditionalCheckFailedException leads to 'continue'. Does not mention the retry-duplicate path or the messageId key.

finding.summary: runId is generated with randomUUID() inside the retry loop, so each retry attempt carries a different runId and the consumer cannot identify duplicates.
finding.evidence: randomUUID() appears in the enqueueRun function near the retry loop.

finding.summary: The per-record try/except swallows every exception and the handler returns normally, so Lambda reports the whole batch as successful and SQS deletes all messages. The new DLQ with maxReceiveCount=3 can never fire: failed runs are not retried and poison messages are dropped with only a log line. The handler must return batchItemFailures (ReportBatchItemFailures) for failed ids.
finding.evidence: handler.py catches Exception, logs, and returns {'processed': len(Records)} without a batchItemFailures list; queues.ts adds deadLetterQueue maxReceiveCount 3 but nothing in the diff enables partial batch response.

finding.summary: Catching all exceptions in the handler means failed messages are acknowledged and deleted, so errors are only visible in logs.
finding.evidence: Right idea about swallowed failures, but no link to the DLQ never receiving messages or to the missing batchItemFailures response.

finding.summary: maxReceiveCount=3 is too low for an agent workload: transient model API errors will push healthy messages to the DLQ prematurely; it should be raised to 10 or more.
finding.evidence: deadLetterQueue sets maxReceiveCount: 3.

finding.summary: The quota check is not atomic and reserves nothing: check_and_reserve only reads usage, and record() does get_item then an unconditional put_item. With asyncio.gather launching all subtasks concurrently (and multiple ECS tasks), every subtask passes the check against the same stale value and concurrent record() calls overwrite each other, so a tenant can overshoot the limit and stored usage under-counts. Needs an atomic ADD with a ConditionExpression.
finding.evidence: quota.py check_and_reserve has no write; record reads then writes tokens + item; orchestrator.py gathers one() coroutines that each call check_and_reserve before any record() has run.

finding.summary: record() reads the current token count and writes back count + tokens with put_item, so concurrent updates overwrite each other and usage is under-counted.
finding.evidence: Identifies the lost-update in record() but does not address the check-then-act race in check_and_reserve or the parallel subtasks.

finding.summary: The quota day boundary uses UTC (gmtime), so tenants in other timezones see their daily quota reset mid-working-day; it should use the tenant's local day.
finding.evidence: _day() formats time.gmtime().

finding.summary: A blind tenacity retry wraps create_ticket, a non-idempotent POST with no idempotency key. A ReadTimeout (5s read timeout) often happens after the server already created the ticket, so each retry creates another one: up to 4 duplicate tickets per tool call, on top of any retry the agent loop does when the tool errors.
finding.evidence: The @retry decorator retries on httpx.ReadTimeout with stop_after_attempt(4); the httpx.post body and headers contain only Authorization and the payload, with no Idempotency-Key or dedupe field.

finding.summary: Retrying create_ticket is unsafe.
finding.evidence: Bare assertion with no steps.

finding.summary: wait_exponential has no jitter, so many concurrent agents retrying a flaky ticket API will hit it in synchronized waves (thundering herd).
finding.evidence: wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=0.5, max=8) is used rather than wait_random_exponential.

finding.summary: min(top_k, 50) silently truncates results, so a caller asking for 100 chunks gets 50 with no error or signal, a hidden contract change.
finding.evidence: The LIMIT parameter is min(top_k, 50).

finding.summary: The 'while True' agent loop is unbounded and can run forever, consuming tokens without limit if the model keeps requesting tools.
finding.evidence: The loop header is while True.

finding.summary: Promise.all means a single failing summarizeChunk rejects the whole call and discards every other chunk summary, so one bad chunk fails the document.
finding.evidence: The fan-out uses Promise.all over picked.map.

finding.summary: A 30 minute visibilityTimeout is far too long: when a worker dies, the message stays invisible for half an hour before retry, delaying recovery of failed runs.
finding.evidence: visibilityTimeout is Duration.minutes(30).

finding.summary: Retrying the ticket POST on timeouts can create duplicate tickets when the first request actually succeeded server-side.
finding.evidence: The for-attempt loop re-sends httpx.post after ReadTimeout.

finding.summary: Deduplication should key on the SQS messageId rather than msg.runId; a producer-supplied id can be reused or spoofed and SQS already assigns a unique id.
finding.evidence: The key is built from run#${msg.runId} instead of record.messageId.

finding.summary: Accessibility defects: the clickable div and retry div have no role, tabindex or keyboard handler so they are unreachable by keyboard, the img has no alt text, the icon-only retry has no accessible name, and the note input has no label and its focus outline is removed.
finding.evidence: MessageRow.tsx uses div onClick without role/tabIndex, img without alt, svg-only control, input with only a placeholder; chat.css sets .note:focus outline none.

finding.summary: Circular import: format.ts imports runTool from tools.ts while tools.ts now imports formatToolResult from format.ts. runAndFormat in format.ts also duplicates runToolFormatted in tools.ts.
finding.evidence: format.ts line 1 imports './tools'; tools.ts line 1 imports './format'; both files define the same runTool+formatToolResult composition.

finding.summary: Authorization hole: POST /admin/reindex/:tenantId only uses requireAuth, and requireRole is defined but never applied, so any authenticated user of any role or tenant can trigger a reindex for any tenantId.
finding.evidence: The route is registered with requireAuth only and takes tenantId from req.params without comparing it to req.user; requireRole in auth.ts is not used anywhere in the diff.

finding.summary: Test quality: score is mocked so ranking is never exercised, test_rank_prefers_exact_match prints instead of asserting, test_rank_is_fast depends on wall-clock timing after a time.sleep(2), and test_rank_handles_empty swallows every exception so it cannot fail.
finding.evidence: The diff shows print(result) with no assert, a bare try/except Exception: pass, and a timing assertion following time.sleep(2).

finding.summary: SQL injection: the sort query parameter is interpolated into the ORDER BY clause with an f-string and is not validated against an allow-list, so a caller can inject arbitrary SQL.
finding.evidence: sort: str = Query('created_at') is placed directly in f'... ORDER BY {sort} DESC' while only tenant_id and q are parameterized.

finding.summary: Sensitive data exposure: the request-logging middleware writes dict(request.headers) to logs, leaking Authorization headers and cookies; complete prompts and messages are also logged in complete().
finding.evidence: log.info('request %s %s headers=%s', ..., dict(request.headers)) logs all headers unredacted; client.py logs system and messages at info level.
